items.title: The endpoint of a titration is NOT the equivalence point
items.claim: Titrate vinegar with sodium hydroxide using phenolphthalein. The colour changes when you've added enough base — that's the endpoint. Strictly, the equivalence point (exactly stoichiometric) and the endpoint (when the indicator changes) are two different things.
items.prompt: Why use phenolphthalein with weak-acid + strong-base titrations?

options.text: Its colour change at pH 8.2-10.0 matches the steep pH jump that occurs near the equivalence point in a weak-acid + strong-base titration; choosing the right indicator makes endpoint approximately equal to equivalence point

items.reveal:
A titration of ethanoic acid (pKa 4.76) with NaOH has equivalence point pH around 8.7 (not 7! — the conjugate base CH3COO- is itself basic). Phenolphthalein, with its colour change between pH 8.2 and 10, brackets this.

Methyl orange (pH 3.1-4.4) would change colour FAR before the equivalence point and give a wrong result for the acid concentration.

A strong acid + strong base titration has equivalence at pH 7 with a very steep pH jump — almost any indicator works. A weak acid + weak base titration has no sharp pH jump at all and is usually monitored with a pH meter, not an indicator.
items.why: Titrations are presented as if indicator change marks the answer exactly. The match between indicator pKa and equivalence pH determines accuracy.

items.title: Endpoint and equivalence point are NOT the same
items.claim: Add NaOH to vinegar with phenolphthalein indicator. The pink colour appears when you've added 'enough' base — that's the endpoint. The equivalence point (exactly stoichiometric H+ matches OH-) is at pH 8.7, not pH 7, and the endpoint depends on the indicator you choose.
items.prompt: Why do you pick phenolphthalein specifically for a weak-acid + strong-base titration?

options.text: Phenolphthalein's transition range (pH 8.2-10.0) brackets the equivalence point of weak-acid + strong-base titrations and lies on the steepest part of the pH curve — so endpoint approximately equals equivalence point

items.reveal:
Titrating ethanoic acid (pKa 4.76) with NaOH gives an equivalence point at pH ~8.7 — not 7. The conjugate base CH3COO- is itself slightly basic and shifts the equivalence point above neutral.

Phenolphthalein (8.2-10.0) brackets this and changes colour in the steep part of the pH jump. Methyl orange (3.1-4.4) would change colour FAR before the equivalence point and give a wrong concentration.

A strong-acid + strong-base titration has equivalence at pH 7 with a very steep jump — almost any indicator works. A weak-acid + weak-base titration has no sharp jump at all and is usually monitored with a pH meter, not an indicator.

Calibration of standards, indicator choice, and meniscus reading all contribute to accuracy of the recorded endpoint volume.
items.why: Titrations are presented as if indicator change marks the answer exactly. The match between indicator pKa and equivalence pH determines accuracy.

items.title: A buffer works best when pH = pKa — even though that means it's only half-effective
items.claim: A buffer is maximally effective at resisting pH change when [HA] = [A-], which means pH = pKa by Henderson-Hasselbalch. Counter-intuitively, this is when only half the acid is dissociated — not when you've added the most base.
items.prompt: Why does maximum buffering happen at half-neutralisation?

options.text: Because half-neutralisation is the only stable condition
Adding acid converts A- to HA and vice versa; the ratio [HA]/[A-] changes most slowly when the two are equal — small additions barely shift the log of the ratio, so pH barely changes
Buffers cannot work outside pH = pKa
Acid and base cancel only at pKa

items.reveal:
Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]).

If [HA] = [A-] (i.e. pH = pKa), then log term = 0 and small changes in [A-] or [HA] barely shift pH. Capacity is maximised within ±1 pH unit of pKa.

Move far from pKa and a buffer collapses: at pH = pKa + 2, [A-]/[HA] = 100; adding more acid takes it from 100 to 50 — only a 0.3 pH change at first, but the conjugate base is rapidly used up.

This is why biological buffers are tuned to the physiological pH they need to defend: phosphate (pKa2 = 7.2) inside cells, carbonate-bicarbonate (open system at pH 7.4) in blood. Choosing pKa to match the target pH is buffer design 101.
items.why: Maximum effectiveness coincides with 'only half the acid is reacted' — a useful surprise that follows directly from the log.
